source_refs.note: Topic 4.2, printed pages 93-94: carbon, covalent, ionic and hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions.

blocks.text: Different types of bonds and interactions play vital roles in the structure and function of biological molecules. Carbon is the basic element of organic molecules. It is tetravalent and can react with many other known elements such as H, O, N, P and S. The carbon-hydrogen bond (C-H bond) is the potential source of chemical energy for cellular activities. The carbon-oxygen association in glycosidic linkages gives stability to complex carbohydrate molecules. Carbon combines with nitrogen in amino acid linkages to form peptide bonds and so forms proteins, which are very important because of their diversity in structure and function.
Covalent bonds form when two atoms share electrons. These bonds are often found in organic molecules like proteins and nucleic acids, providing stability to the molecules.

blocks.alt: Two atoms, A (red) and B (blue), each a nucleus with one shell of electrons; each has one unpaired valence electron, joined by a curved double arrow. An arrow leads to the covalent molecule, where the two shells overlap and share the pair of electrons. Labels: Unpaired Valence Electrons, Atom 1, Atom 2, Sharing of Available Valence Electrons, Covalent Molecule.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.1: Covalent bond between two atoms (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.1).

blocks.text: Ionic bonds form when one atom donates an electron (becoming a positive ion, or cation) and another atom accepts the electron (becoming a negative ion, or anion). The electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions forms the ionic bond. Ionic bonds are relatively strong in the solid state and are formed mostly in inorganic molecules like sodium chloride.

blocks.alt: A sodium atom (electrons 2, 8, 1) and a chlorine atom (2, 8, 7) with their shells; a curved arrow carries sodium's single outer electron to chlorine. After the reaction arrow: Na+ with shells 2, 8 and Cl- with shells 2, 8, 8. Labels: Na, Cl, Sodium atom, Chlorine atom, Na+, Cl-, Sodium chloride.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.2: Ionic bond between sodium and chlorine atoms (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.2).

blocks.text: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between a hydrogen atom and an electronegative atom (such as oxygen or nitrogen). These bonds are important in maintaining the structure of large molecules like proteins and nucleic acids, and in various biological processes such as DNA replication.

blocks.alt: Five water molecules drawn as a large red O with two small blue H. Dashed lines join an H of one molecule to the O of a neighbouring molecule. Each O is marked delta minus and the bonded H atoms delta plus.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.3: Hydrogen bond between water molecules (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.3).

blocks.text: Hydrophobic interactions occur between non-polar molecules and polar molecules (like water). Non-polar molecules tend to cluster together in aqueous environments to minimise contact with water molecules. This phenomenon is crucial for the folding of proteins and the formation of lipid bilayers in cell membranes.

Hydrophilic interactions occur between polar molecules and water molecules. They are essential for the dissolution of polar and ionic compounds in water, and they help in various biological processes such as nutrient transport and chemical reactions within cells.
